title: Is Subsequence
directAnswer: Walk a pointer through `t`; every time the current `t` character matches the next needed `s` character, advance the `s` pointer. `s` is a subsequence iff its pointer reaches the end. O(n) time, O(1) space. For the follow-up (many `s` queries against one fixed `t`), preprocess `t` into per-character sorted index lists and binary-search each query.

rules: **Advance the `s` pointer only on a match**; always advance through `t`. Order within `s` must be preserved, so greedy first-match is safe.
**`s` is a subsequence iff its pointer reaches `len(s)`** — i.e. every character of `s` was matched in order.
**Greedy is provably correct**: taking the earliest matching position in `t` never blocks a later match (it leaves the most of `t` available).
**Empty `s` is trivially a subsequence** of any `t` — the loop matches zero characters and `i == 0 == len(s)`.
**For many queries on the same `t`, preprocess once** into char → sorted indices and binary-search, turning each query into `O(|s|·log|t|)`.
whenToUse: Check whether one sequence appears in another while preserving relative order (not contiguity)
Single linear pass suffices and order matters but gaps are allowed
Many queries against a fixed text → preprocess once, answer each fast
antiSignals: You need a CONTIGUOUS match (substring) → that's strStr/KMP, not subsequence
You need the LONGEST common subsequence of two strings → LCS dynamic programming
You need to count distinct subsequences → counting DP, not a membership check
Characters can be reordered freely → that's an anagram/multiset question
remember.takeaway: Subsequence membership is the textbook two-pointer greedy: scan the haystack `t`, consume `s` in order, and you're done in O(n). The interview depth lives in the follow-up — when `t` is fixed and you face many `s` queries, amortize by preprocessing `t` into index lists (binary search) or a next-position DP table.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize order-preserving membership as a one-pass two-pointer greedy, and whether you can extend it efficiently to the 'many queries, fixed t' follow-up.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Confusing subsequence with substring (requiring contiguity), or advancing the s pointer even on a mismatch. For the follow-up, re-scanning t per query instead of preprocessing it once.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Nail the two-pointer in O(n), then proactively raise the follow-up: 'if there are many s queries against one t, I'd preprocess t into per-character sorted index lists and binary-search, or build a next-position DP table.'

problemStatement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `s` is a **subsequence** of `t`, or `false` otherwise.

A **subsequence** of a string is a new string that is formed from the original string by deleting some (can be none) of the characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters. (i.e., `"ace"` is a subsequence of `"abcde"` while `"aec"` is not.)

**Follow up:** Suppose there are lots of incoming `s`, say `s1, s2, ..., sk` where `k >= 10⁹`, and you want to check one by one to see if `t` has its subsequence. In this scenario, how would you change your code?
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters
understanding: We must confirm that every character of s appears in t in the same left-to-right order, allowing arbitrary gaps (deletions) in t. It's an order-preserving membership test, not a contiguous-substring test.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the match need to be contiguous?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Subsequence allows gaps; only relative order must be preserved. 'ace' is a subsequence of 'abcde'. Contiguity would make it a substring problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if s is empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: An empty string is a subsequence of anything → return true. The two-pointer handles it naturally since the s pointer starts already 'done'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there many s queries against the same t?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: That's the explicit follow-up. If so, preprocess t once into per-character sorted index lists (binary search) or a next-position DP table, instead of re-scanning t for every query.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Only lowercase letters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a fixed alphabet of 26, which makes the preprocessed DP table (26 columns) cheap and attractive for the follow-up.

diagrams.title: Two-pointer greedy match
diagrams.caption: Pointer j scans t; pointer i advances through s only when characters match.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — Greedy Linear Scan (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. It's the natural single-query answer and the baseline you'll extend for the follow-up.
hints: You need the characters of s to appear in t in order. If you scan t once, what should you do each time you see the next character of s you're looking for?
Keep an index i into s. Walk t left to right; whenever t's current character equals s[i], move i forward — you've matched that character of s.
If i reaches len(s), every character of s was matched in order → true. If t runs out first, → false.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass over t (length n), with the s pointer advancing at most |s| times → O(n) time. Only two integer pointers are used → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Subsequence membership is the archetypal **two-pointer greedy**. We keep a pointer `i` marking the next character of `s` we still need to find, and we sweep a pointer through `t`. Each time `t`'s current character equals `s[i]`, we've satisfied that character of `s`, so we advance `i`. When the sweep ends, `s` is a subsequence exactly when `i` has reached `len(s)` — meaning every character of `s` found a home in `t`, in order.

**Why we only advance `i` on a match.** The defining property of a subsequence is *order preservation*. The `i` pointer must move strictly forward through `s` and only when the current `t` character is the one `s` needs next. We never rewind `i`, because a subsequence can't reuse or reorder characters. Meanwhile the `t` pointer always advances — a non-matching `t` character is simply a 'deletion' we skip over, which is allowed.

**Why greedy (earliest match) is provably correct.** A natural worry: by grabbing the *first* occurrence of `s[i]` in `t`, could we accidentally consume a character we'd have needed later, blocking a valid match? No — and the exchange argument is clean. Suppose some valid matching pairs `s[i]` with a *later* position `p` in `t`. Taking the *earliest* position `q ≤ p` instead leaves the suffix `t[q+1:]` ⊇ `t[p+1:]`, so anything the later choice could still match, the earlier choice can match too. **Earliest-match never reduces future options**, so greedy is safe. This is why we don't need backtracking or DP for a single query.

**Why the empty-`s` and exhausted-`t` cases just work.** If `s` is empty, `i` starts at `0 == len(s)` and the final check returns true without matching anything — correct, since the empty string is everyone's subsequence. If `t` is exhausted before `i` reaches the end, the loop stops and `i < len(s)` yields false. The `i < len(s)` guard inside the loop also prevents indexing past the end of `s` once we've already matched all of it.
approaches.insight: Order-preserving membership = scan the long string once, consume the short string greedily. The earliest-match exchange argument is the proof that greedy beats DP here for a single query — worth stating to show you know *why* it's correct, not just that it works.

approaches.name: Preprocess t — Index Lists + Binary Search (Follow-up: Many Queries)
approaches.whenToMention: Raise this for the stated follow-up: k ≥ 10⁹ queries s1…sk against one fixed t. Preprocess t once, answer each query fast.

complexity.time: O(|t|) preprocess, then O(|s|·log|t|) per query

hints: If t is fixed and you'll test thousands of s strings, re-scanning all of t per query is wasteful. What could you compute about t ONCE to speed up each query?

For each character, store the sorted list of indices where it appears in t. Then matching s greedily becomes: 'find the smallest index of s[i] in t that is strictly greater than where I matched the previous character.'
That 'smallest index greater than prev' is an upper-bound binary search on the character's index list. If any character has no such index, s isn't a subsequence.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building char → sorted index lists is one pass over t → O(|t|) time and space. Each query does, per character of s, one binary search over that character's index list → O(|s|·log|t|). Across many queries the O(|t|) build is amortized away.
approaches.explanation:
The follow-up changes the economics: with `k ≥ 10⁹` queries against a *single fixed* `t`, the O(|t|) per-query scan from the two-pointer approach becomes the bottleneck. The fix is to **pay an O(|t|) preprocessing cost once** and make each query sublinear in `|t|`.

**The preprocessing.** Scan `t` once and, for each character, record the sorted list of positions where it occurs. For `t = "abcabc"`, we'd store `a → [0, 3]`, `b → [1, 4]`, `c → [2, 5]`. Because we append while scanning left to right, each list is automatically sorted ascending.

**Answering a query with binary search.** We track `prev`, the index in `t` where we matched the previous character of `s` (initially `-1`). For each character `c` of the query, we need the *smallest* position of `c` in `t` that is *strictly greater* than `prev` — that's an upper-bound (`bisect_right`) search on `c`'s index list. If `c` never appears, or every occurrence is `≤ prev`, the search falls off the end and `s` is not a subsequence. Otherwise we set `prev` to that position and continue. This mirrors the greedy earliest-match logic of the two-pointer version, but jumps directly to the next valid position instead of scanning over the gaps.

**Why this is the right amortization.** Preprocessing is `O(|t|)` once. Then each query costs `O(|s| · log|t|)` — for short `s` (≤ 100 here) that's tiny, and crucially independent of how much of `t` lies between matches. Over `k` queries the total is `O(|t| + Σ|s_i|·log|t|)`, vastly better than `O(k·|t|)`.

**The DP alternative — next-position table.** Because the alphabet is a fixed 26 letters, an even slicker preprocessing is a **next-position DP table**: `nxt[i][c]` = the smallest index `≥ i` in `t` where character `c` occurs (or a sentinel if none). Build it right-to-left in `O(|t|·26)`. Each query then becomes a pure `O(|s|)` walk: from position `pos`, jump to `nxt[pos][s[k]] + 1`, with no binary search at all. This is the dynamic-programming framing of the same idea and is often the cleanest answer to give for the follow-up when the alphabet is small and fixed.
approaches.insight: When one structure (t) is queried many times, shift work from per-query to one-time preprocessing. Index-lists-plus-binary-search and the 26-column next-position DP table are two encodings of the same 'jump to the next occurrence' idea — the latter trades a little build cost for O(|s|) queries with no logs.

commonMistakes: Confusing subsequence (gaps allowed) with substring (must be contiguous).
Advancing the s pointer on a mismatch instead of only on a match.
Indexing s without an i < len(s) guard once s is fully matched.
For the many-queries follow-up, re-scanning all of t per query instead of preprocessing it once.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the s pointer on a mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Moving i when characters differ breaks the order-preserving match and can wrongly accept or reject; i must move only on a match.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating it like a substring search
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Subsequence allows skipping characters in t. Requiring a contiguous block (e.g. t.contains(s)) rejects valid cases like s='ace', t='abcde'.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return t.contains(s);   // wrong: demands a contiguous substring

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Re-scanning t per query (follow-up)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With k ≥ 10⁹ queries, an O(|t|) scan each time is O(k·|t|). Preprocess t once into index lists and binary-search per query instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# build idx = char -> sorted positions ONCE for fixed t,
# then each query is O(|s| log |t|) via bisect (see optimal approach)

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: When you need the longest shared subsequence (not just membership), two pointers no longer suffice — use 2D DP.

followupVariations.title: Number of Matching Subsequences
followupVariations.hint: Exactly the many-queries follow-up: bucket words by their next-needed char or preprocess t and answer each.

followupVariations.title: Distinct Subsequences
followupVariations.hint: Count how many ways s appears as a subsequence of t — counting DP, a step beyond membership.

patternNote: Two-pointer greedy for order-preserving membership: scan t once, consume s on matches, O(n). The follow-up (many queries on a fixed t) is the real interview depth — preprocess t into per-character sorted index lists (binary search) or a 26-column next-position DP table to make each query sublinear in |t|. Related: Number of Matching Subsequences and Longest Common Subsequence.
